planting.note: Pot offsets (pups) in coarse, fast-draining bark mix once they reach a few inches tall; grow as a houseplant or on a shaded frost-free patio.

directions: This Brazilian and Paraguayan epiphyte forms a narrow upright tube of dull green, mealy-banded leaves edged in small spines, closely related to the familiar queen's tears but taller and more columnar. Grow it in bright, filtered light such as high open shade beneath trees or an east-facing window, since direct sun bleaches the foliage while deep shade weakens flowering. In spring the drooping flower spike opens green petals margined in violet beneath large rose-pink bracts, a striking contrast against the tube-shaped rosette. Keep the central cup topped with rainwater and let the potting mix dry slightly between waterings.

planting.note: Grow mounted on a tree limb or potted in chunky, fast-draining bark mix under high canopy shade; protect from temperatures below 45°F.

directions: Native to the deciduous and semi-deciduous forests of Mexico, Central America, Colombia, and Ecuador, this large tank-forming epiphyte grows naturally on tree trunks from sea level to over 5,000 feet. It forms a broad funnel-shaped rosette of strap-shaped leaves that holds rainwater in its central cup, and produces a tall terminal spike with colorful triangular bracts above small tubular flowers. Because it comes from forest interiors, dappled light under high tree canopy or bright shade on a porch suits it far better than open sun. Flush the central cup periodically with fresh water and allow the bark-based growing medium to dry somewhat between waterings to avoid rot.

planting.note: Mount on a branch with sphagnum or pot in open bark mix; keep in dappled forest-floor-style shade year-round.

directions: Widespread from southern Mexico through Central America into northern South America, this compact epiphytic bromeliad grows wild in humid wet-tropical forest understories, attached to trunks and branches rather than in soil. The slender, arching leaves resemble an oversized Tillandsia, and the inflorescence carries bright red floral bracts with yellow flowers that persist showily as fruit develops. It wants partial shade and steady humidity rather than the strong light favored by sun-form bromeliads, making it a good fit for a shaded lanai or greenhouse bench. Mist regularly and keep the small central cup filled with clean water.
sources: Kew Plants of the World Online (POWO)

planting.note: Mount on bark or cork in high humidity; grow under shade cloth or tree canopy rather than open sun, which this montane forest species cannot tolerate.

directions: This montane rainforest epiphyte from the Andes and Amazon basin grows between roughly 2,600 and 11,000 feet elevation, typically clinging to moss-covered branches in cool, cloud-wrapped forest interiors. Multiple branching spikes carry rose, purple, or blue tubular flowers over many months, and the foliage reddens somewhat when grown bright but cool. Because it is adapted to constant humidity and indirect light under a closed canopy, it performs best in shaded greenhouse or terrarium conditions with frequent misting rather than full sun. Unlike many xeric Tillandsia, it does not go dormant and continues flowering on the same rosette for several years without dying back.
sources: Kew Plants of the World Online (POWO)
Selbyana journal — Colombian Andean cloud forest Tillandsia phenology study
Bromeliad Society of Australia photo index

planting.note: Mount on bark in a shaded highland-forest setup; seedlings establish only under humid, filtered light, not open sun.

directions: Native to the cool highland forests of Chiapas, Guatemala, and neighboring Central America, this spineless epiphyte develops long, purple-tinged leaves and is named for its vivid pink quill-like floral bracts, which rise well above the foliage on a spike holding small tubular flowers. Research on its establishment in Chiapas cloud forest shows it depends on filtered humidity and light rather than open exposure, so growers should site it in high dappled shade such as under tree canopy or shade cloth. It is noticeably larger than most garden Tillandsia, with mature rosettes reaching several feet across in habitat. Keep humidity high and mist regularly, letting excess water drain away to prevent crown rot.
sources: Scielo Costa Rica — humidity, nutrients and light in Tillandsia guatemalensis establishment study
Kew Plants of the World Online (POWO)
Wikipedia species account cross-referenced with GBIF occurrence data

planting.note: Pot offsets in open bark-based mix; keep in filtered shade and protect from temperatures below 34°F.

directions: Endemic to the Atlantic Forest of southeastern Brazil, this clustering epiphyte takes its name from the powdery white farina that coats its bright pink to reddish-brown leaves, which form a dense, flattened rosette of about twenty leaves. It is distinctly more shade-dependent than many showy Neoregelia cultivars, requiring filtered forest-floor-style shade to avoid scorching and to keep the farina intact. Small violet flowers appear low in the central cup, nearly hidden by the surrounding foliage in classic Neoregelia fashion. Keep the cup filled with clean water and propagate readily from the offsets that cluster around the base.
sources: Kew Plants of the World Online (POWO)

planting.note: Grow in a large pot of coarse bark mix under bright shade; this is a big species, so allow ample room for the spreading rosette.

directions: Endemic to the Atlantic Forest of Brazil with a disjunct population in Venezuela, this large Vriesea forms a wide spreading rosette of broad green leaves, each tipped with a distinctive dark, tar-like spot that gives the species its common and scientific names. A stout, erect flower spike rising over a yard tall carries many lax, sticky-glutinous flowers with orange-red petals, held well above the foliage. Like most forest Vriesea, it wants bright indirect light rather than direct sun, which quickly scorches the broad, soft leaves. Keep the central tank filled with water and site it where its considerable spread will not crowd neighboring shade plants.
sources: Bromeliad Society International Cultivar Registry parentage notes

planting.note: Pot in open bark mix and keep in low to moderate light; among the most shade-tolerant Vriesea for a dim windowsill or shaded lanai.

directions: Endemic to Brazil's Atlantic Forest, this compact Vriesea stays small compared to its showier relatives, with green leaves marked by maroon to nearly black bases that form a tight rosette. Flattened, paddle-like inflorescence spikes rise on slender stems and range from solid red to tricolor combinations of green, yellow, and red depending on the individual plant. It tolerates noticeably lower light than most tank bromeliads, making it a good candidate for genuinely shady spots such as a north-facing room or deep porch shade where brighter Vriesea would fail to color well. Keep the small central cup topped with water and avoid overly bright exposure, which can bleach the maroon leaf bases.
sources: Bromeliad Society International Cultivar Registry ('White Cloud' variegate parentage notes)
Wikipedia species account cross-referenced with Tropicos

planting.note: Pot offsets in bark-based mix under filtered or dense shade; the pale spotting is most pronounced out of direct sun.

directions: Endemic to Brazil's rainforest understory, this compact Neoregelia carries reddish-brown inner leaves speckled with pale green spots, a pattern that distinguishes it from similar species with darker spotting. Like other forest-floor Neoregelia, it grows as a canopy-dwelling epiphyte in deep shade in the wild, using leaf litter and rainfall collected in its central cup for nutrition rather than soil roots. Small flowers remain tucked low in the water-holding cup, typical of the genus, rarely rising above the surrounding leaves. Keep it out of direct sun, which fades the spotted pattern, and maintain a clean, topped-off cup of water for best growth.
